cancel_download is not yet called from any web route or MCP tool in this repo (verified via repo-wide grep); once it is wired to an external caller, that call site should be checked for authorization/IDOR (i.e. whether the caller verifies the requester owns the given username/transfer_id pair) since slskd itself provides no such check.

cancel_download follows the patterns already in SlskdTransferClient. It builds the URL from the module constant _TRANSFERS_DOWNLOAD_ROOT, encodes segments with quote(..., safe=""), sends the request through the shared _request_json helper, and turns a non-dict result into {}. enqueue_download and get_user_downloads (src/roonseek/transfer.py:178-202) do the same. No pattern-consistency gate is met.

The new keyword-only success_statuses parameter on _request_json is a small, backward-compatible extension. Callers that leave it out keep the old {200, 201} behavior through `success_statuses or {200, 201}`. The auth (401/403), 429 and 5xx handling still runs first, so DELETE gets the same error classification. A 204 or other empty-body response is already handled by the existing `if not response.content: return {}` check at line 266, so the 204 success code is safe.

Minor semantic note, not a finding because the issue is pre-existing: a cancel that fails with an unexpected status raises TransferEnqueueError, even though it is not an enqueue. get_user_downloads (GET) already has the same naming mismatch, so the diff follows the established behavior. Behavioral note for the bugs/impact lanes, not architecture: a 404 on DELETE (transfer already gone or already removed) is not in the success set. No new dependencies, no import cycles, no cross-module reach-in. The diff only touches src/roonseek/transfer.py. A grep of src/ for other HTTP DELETE calls or success_statuses-style overrides found none, so no competing pattern exists.

agent_notes: Public API: the change is additive only. `_request_json` gains an optional keyword-only `success_statuses` that defaults to None, which falls back to {200, 201}. The existing callers, enqueue_download (transfer.py:187) and get_user_downloads (transfer.py:197), behave exactly as before. slskd.py has its own separate _request_json and is unaffected.
`success_statuses or {200, 201}`: an empty set would also fall back to the default. No caller passes one, so this is harmless.
A 204 or empty-body response returns {} through the existing `if not response.content` branch (transfer.py:266), so the 204 success path works and doesn't raise a JSON error.

The username and transfer_id are both percent-encoded with safe='', which matches the existing T-02-02 path-injection control. tests/test_transfer.py:292 covers the encoding of '/' and spaces. The 401/403/5xx handling, including the sanitized messages that don't echo the API key, is reused unchanged.

Blast radius: transfer.py is imported by cli.py, pipeline.py, web/pipeline_runner.py, scripts/m001_live_proof.py and three test modules. None of them call cancel_download yet; the only consumer is a test fake (tests/test_jobs_api.py:520) for the Phase 22-03 failing tests. Production impact for now is limited to the new method.

Naming and taxonomy: cancel failures are raised as TransferEnqueueError, an enqueue-named error class. Callers that catch TransferEnqueueError to mean 'enqueue failed' (for example in the pipeline) would treat a cancel failure the same way if the code paths ever share a handler. Low risk, but worth keeping in mind when wiring 22-03.
Performance: one synchronous HTTP DELETE per cancel, with the existing bounded timeout. No scale concerns. No DB, schema or migration changes.
Verdict: this is a safe additive change and can ship. The open questions are how 404 is handled and whether to pass remove=true, both to settle when the 22-03 cancel caller is wired up.

findings.title: `or`-based Optional fallback treats an explicit empty set as None
